column1: # The vocabulary. Plain definitions, no links: the point is to stop bluffing in briefs.

column3: note
How long an action takes. The single biggest lever on how something feels.
How far a thing moves between frames. Timing says how long, spacing says how fast it feels.
The curve that describes acceleration in and out of a move. Linear reads as mechanical.
A small move opposite to the main action, so the eye is ready for it.
Parts of an object that keep moving after the main mass stops.
Different parts arriving at different times, instead of everything landing on one frame.
Deforming a shape to sell weight and impact while preserving volume.
Natural movement travels on curves, not straight lines.
Composing the frame so the audience looks at the one thing that matters.
A supporting move that enriches the main one without competing with it.
Pushing past the literal to make the read clearer, not merely louder.
Whether the thing is pleasant to look at. Vague, unfashionable, and real.
The impression of mass, communicated almost entirely through timing and easing.
A recorded value at a point in time. Everything between them is interpolated.
How the software fills the frames between keyframes: linear, bezier, hold.
Where you edit the speed and value curves directly, rather than guessing at handles.
A keyframe with no interpolation: the value jumps. The basis of frame-by-frame in a keyframed tool.
Seeing neighbouring frames faintly, so you can draw or place against them.
An animation whose last frame flows into its first. Seamlessness is a timing problem.
Frame-by-frame drawing, named for the transparent celluloid sheets it used to need.
Building controls onto artwork so it can be posed and animated without redrawing.
Attaching one layer's transform to another so it inherits the movement.
An invisible layer that exists only to be parented to and animated.
A small script driving a property, so motion is computed rather than keyframed.
A composition nested inside another. The main tool for keeping a project sane.
A layer used to define what is visible in another layer.
Using one layer's alpha or luminance to cut out another.
The transparency information carried alongside colour.
Combining separate rendered elements into one convincing image.
Tracing or masking footage frame by frame to isolate part of it.
Extracting movement from footage so new elements can be attached to it.
A single still that establishes the look of a sequence before anything moves.
The shot-by-shot plan. Cheaper to fix here than anywhere downstream.
The storyboard cut to timing, usually with scratch audio. The first honest look at pace.
An animatic built straight from boards, before any animation exists.
The document that sells the direction. Often the actual deliverable of week one.
Frames per second. 24 for film feel, 25 or 30 for broadcast, 60 for interfaces.
Pixel dimensions of the frame. Not the same thing as quality.
The frame's proportions. 16:9, 1:1, 9:16: plan for all three from the start.
How the video is compressed. ProRes to edit, H.264 to deliver, rarely both.
How many values each colour channel can hold. 8-bit banding is the usual symptom.
The defined range of colour a file describes: sRGB, Rec.709, and the source of most mismatches.
Turning the project into frames. Also the thing that always takes longer than the estimate.
A JSON format that carries vector animation into apps and the web at any size.
Trading colour depth for texture with a pattern of pixels. The club's house look.
Motion generated by rules and parameters rather than by hand-set keyframes.
